relationship: Children dashed in judgment against Babylon
rationale: The psalm’s violent blessing concerning Babylon’s infants corresponds to Isaiah’s Babylon oracle describing their children dashed before them. Isaiah does not specify the psalm’s rock.

relationship: Preservation amid affliction and hostile power
rationale: Psalm 137 anticipates being kept alive if the speaker walks amid affliction and recalls God stretching His hand against the enemies’ anger and saving him with His right hand. Psalm 17 recalls enemies overtaking him on the day of affliction and the Lord becoming his support and bringing him into a spacious place; it also expresses future assurances of rescue. The conditional expectation and remembered acts remain distinct; the right-hand image belongs to Psalm 137.
Both passages combine divine holding and guidance. Psalm 138 says God’s right hand will hold the speaker; Psalm 72 says God grasped the speaker’s right hand and guided him in counsel.

relationship: Goliath’s challenge in the named heading
rationale: The source heading explicitly concerns Goliath; the account in 1 Samuel names Goliath and records his challenge to Israel for single combat. This identifies the named narrative figure without requiring every poetic battle image to be a literal detail of the encounter.

relationship: Speaking of fearsome works and divine power
rationale: Psalm 144 anticipates speech about the power of God’s fearsome acts and His greatness. Psalm 65 commands speech to God calling His works fearsome, then says His enemies will lie to Him through the abundance of His power. The fearsome-works and power language is shared, while the target’s consequence for enemies is distinct.

relationship: A praise summons with differing goodness clauses
rationale: Both summon praise of the Lord and follow it with a goodness clause. Psalm 146 calls a psalm good and asks that praise please God; Psalm 134 calls the Lord good and commands music to His name, adding “for it is beautiful.” The repeated form is compared without equating the subjects of good or resolving the final it.

relationship: Divine breath or wind controls frost and water
rationale: Psalm 147 says God will send His word and melt them, blow His wind, and waters will flow. Elihu says frost will be given from the Strong One’s breath and He steers water as He wishes. Divine wind or breath and control of water connect the passages, while frost-giving and melting remain different actions.

relationship: Creation endures under God’s established word
rationale: The enduring establishment and command that will not pass away correspond to God’s word remaining in heaven, the founded earth remaining, and the day remaining by His arrangement. The exact subjects and time expressions remain distinct.

relationship: Praise in heavenly and holy assembly language
rationale: Praise among God’s holy ones and in the firmament of His power corresponds to the heavens acknowledging His wonders and His truth in an assembly of holy ones. This does not resolve the identity of every holy one.

The full heading places David’s fight with Goliath in single combat; the account in 1 Samuel identifies Goliath and records his challenge for two men to fight in single combat. The psalm’s outside-the-number statement remains its own heading metadata.
